routes.description: Establish a historically usable body of early testimony concerning Jesus' postmortem appearances and bodily resurrection, then show that an intentional divine resurrection explains that evidence more adequately than the proposed natural mechanisms under a defensible method of historical comparison.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early testimony warrants the relevant appearance and bodily-resurrection claims, the resurrection hypothesis supplies the strongest unified explanation of them, and objections based on hallucination, source unreliability, missing-body alternatives, and antecedent improbability do not defeat that inference.

motionBridge.description: Connect the historically warranted appearance and bodily-resurrection evidence to the conclusion that Jesus rose and that this hypothesis better explains the testimony than naturalistic alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Establish that sufficiently early and historically usable sources report individual and group experiences interpreted as appearances of the risen Jesus and as bodily resurrection.
Show that hallucination, visionary contagion, disappearance, fabrication, and related natural proposals do not jointly match the evidence as well as the resurrection hypothesis.

Justify evaluating competing hypotheses through explanatory scope, power, ad hocness, and plausibility while handling disputed prior probabilities without excluding purposive divine action in advance.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how physical-body considerations, possible grave investigation, and the early proclaimers' sincere commitment constrain disappearance and fabrication accounts.
Defend the historical usability of the Gospel narrative core despite genre conventions, literary development, and discrepancies in peripheral details.

routes.description: Show that the surviving early testimony is sparse, culturally mediated, and compatible with ordinary processes such as visions, social reinforcement, disappearance, and narrative development, while arguing that its evidential force is insufficient to overcome the resurrection hypothesis's weak antecedent support.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if one or more collectively credible natural processes adequately account for the reported testimony without requiring a uniquely reconstructed history, and if source limitations and prior-probability considerations prevent that testimony from making resurrection the better historical explanation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the availability and collective plausibility of natural mechanisms, together with evidential limitations, to rejection of resurrection as the better explanation of early Christian testimony.

centralBridges.description: Establish that religious visions, charismatic suggestion, cultural reinforcement, cognitive processes, and ordinary missing-body scenarios can generate the central reported beliefs and traditions.

Show that a hypothesis involving resurrection requires unusually strong evidence because it lacks established background precedent and depends on prior commitments about divine existence and intention.
Demonstrate that the early epistolary record lacks sufficient detail and that later narrative sources contain features that limit their ability to establish bodily encounters and an empty grave.
Justify historical rejection of resurrection when several collectively likely natural scenarios remain available even if the evidence does not identify one complete natural reconstruction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how sincere believers could infer bodily resurrection without verifying an empty grave or could assimilate contrary physical evidence through prior religious commitments.
Account for the restricted appearance pattern and exceptional conversions as features expected within a localized visionary movement rather than public divine disclosure.

sections.title: Historical Method, Reference Classes, and Prior Probability
sections.rationale: The governing comparison determines whether explanatory criteria may bracket disputed priors or whether resurrection's lack of established precedent imposes an extraordinary evidential threshold; that choice structures every later inference from the testimony.

sections.title: Pauline Testimony and the Bodily Character of Resurrection
sections.rationale: The early Pauline material supplies the principal evidential base for appearances and bodily-resurrection belief, while its chronology, detail, interpretation, and capacity to support physical encounters remain central points of dispute.

sections.title: Visionary, Psychological, and Social-Contagion Explanations
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of individual and group experiences bear directly on whether ordinary religious and social processes can explain the appearance traditions or whether their phenomenology and distribution require a different causal account.

sections.title: Empty Grave, Investigation, and Proclaimer Sincerity
sections.rationale: Questions about disappearance, grave verification, bodily inference, and the costly sincerity of early proclaimers constrain both fabrication accounts and claims that vision-driven belief could develop independently of physical evidence.

sections.title: Historical Usability of the Gospel Narratives
sections.rationale: The status of Gospel detail affects whether empty-tomb and embodied-appearance narratives can supplement the sparse epistolary record, requiring attention to genre, embellishment, literary construction, external support, and contradictions.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Historical hypotheses should be compared by explanatory scope, explanatory power, avoidance of ad hoc assumptions, and plausibility rather than by subjective Bayesian priors.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted affirmative opening statement and explicit first-person framing identify Licona as the speaker.

response.rationale: This constructive move introduces the affirmative's governing criteria for comparing historical explanations and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly and efficiently establishes a framework used by the subsequent affirmative case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The four criteria and their comparative function are recoverable, although the displacement of Bayesian priors is more implicit than fully defended.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The criteria are appropriate comparative tools, but treating subjective priors as dispensable is asserted more broadly than the supplied methodological warrant supports.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparison framework is internally consistent, with one bounded missing bridge concerning how plausibility differs from or incorporates prior probability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The criteria are identified and partly explained, but their superiority to Bayesian treatment is not supported by a substantial methodological comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this directly supplies the historical-method bridge governing the affirmative's explanatory comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span presents an affirmative methodological framework rather than engaging a developed opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly lists explanatory scope and describes historians forming and comparing hypotheses, while the locked proposition supplies the remaining stated criteria and contrast with subjective priors.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Early Pauline material reports individual and group appearances and supports the conclusion that Jesus and future Christians were understood to rise bodily.
moves.attributionBasis: The affirmative opening continues without a speaker transition, using Licona's announced positive historical case.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the affirmative's early testimonial basis and has no earlier opposing locked move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly states the early appearance reports and the claimed bodily interpretation on which the case depends.

precisionFindings.rationale: The bodily-resurrection conclusion is clear, but the movement from Pauline teaching to a transformed physical corpse and physical appearances lacks an explicit interpretive qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The span calls the beliefs and teachings facts, while the sparse quoted Pauline basis does not by itself establish detailed transformed-corpse encounters with comparable certainty.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is usable, but it compresses the material bridge from resurrection vocabulary and appearance lists to detailed bodily encounters.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Early Pauline reporting supports appearances and resurrection belief, but the excerpt does not document the textual steps needed for the stronger physical-corpse conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the move directly supplies the principal testimonial and bodily-resurrection premise for the affirmative route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive presentation states its positive reading without directly testing a developed alternative interpretation in this span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly attributes bodily future resurrection, Jesus' transformed physical corpse, and individual and group appearances to the early teaching, but supplies little textual documentation for those interpretive steps.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: The resurrection hypothesis explains the reported appearances with comprehensive scope and power, without improper ad hocness or exclusion by worldview assumptions.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona explicitly applies the previously introduced criteria and closes his uninterrupted affirmative opening statement.

response.rationale: This constructive move applies the stated criteria to the resurrection hypothesis and has no earlier opposing locked target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it reaches the motion-level comparison directly, though its rival comparison remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory claim is clear, but the scope of all relevant data and the worldview qualification are not bounded sufficiently in the span.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying the hypothesis could not explain the appearances better greatly exceeds a span that asserts scope and power without a serious comparison to alternatives or priors.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Resurrection would entail appearances, but compatibility is treated as explanatory superiority without completing the comparative or prior-probability bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion relies substantially on assertion that the hypothesis accounts for every report without strain and does not document a representative rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the motion tier, this expressly connects the reported appearances to resurrection as the claimed best explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: No natural alternative is developed sufficiently within this selected span to support a distinct charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt applies explanatory scope and power to individual, group, friendly, and hostile appearances and calls the fit unsurpassable, but it does not test that conclusion against a developed natural hypothesis.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Because resurrection lacks established background precedent, the claim that Jesus rose requires evidence comparable to other extraordinary and otherwise unsupported claims.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator has yielded to Carrier, and the first-person comparison explicitly addresses the sufficiency of Mike's evidence.

components.text: Whether explanatory comparison may avoid giving substantial weight to antecedent probability and established background precedent.
Whether asserted explanatory scope and power provide evidence strong enough for the resurrection conclusion.

response.rationale: The starship analogy directly contests the affirmative's treatment of priors and demands unusually strong evidence before its explanatory-fit claim can warrant resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the decisive methodological premise and applies the objection to the resurrection inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The threshold argument is readily recoverable, though extraordinary evidence is left as a comparative standard rather than operationally specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Background precedent is relevant to evidential demands, but equivalence with unsupported starship ownership is stronger than the analogy alone establishes.

charity.alternative: Resurrection may be assessed as a singular purposive event rather than a repeatable natural generalization.
charity.decisiveQualification: A singular intentional hypothesis still requires antecedent support for the agent's existence and intention.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from low established precedent to a heightened evidential threshold is coherent, with a bounded analogy gap concerning intentional divine action.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The absence of an established resurrection reference class supports the concern, but the chosen comparison is illustrative rather than a defended quantitative evidential analysis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this squarely supplies the con route's indispensable evidential-threshold requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument fairly emphasizes missing background support, though the starship analogy compresses the purposive-event distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares resurrection with starship ownership, explicitly cites the lack of supporting generalization, and concludes that the claim requires extraordinary evidence.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Paul's letters portray vision-prone early Christians and do not establish detailed bodily encounters, so their reported appearances are reasonably explained as religious hallucinations.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier explicitly turns from Licona's presentation to the epistles and repeatedly distinguishes his reading from Mike's.

components.text: Whether Pauline material establishes bodily encounters rather than vision-prone religious experiences.

response.rationale: The move directly contests the affirmative's Pauline interpretation by characterizing the early community as regularly ecstatic and by stressing the lack of detailed bodily encounters.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the decisive evidential interpretation, though the bodily-text analysis is less developed than the hallucination context.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternative reading is clear, but hallucinating is used broadly for varied ecstatic phenomena and the inference's population scope is insufficiently bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Vision-proneness makes a visionary account plausible, but the span does not establish that the particular reported appearances were probably hallucinations.

charity.alternative: Paul's resurrection vocabulary and appearance tradition may imply bodily resurrection despite sparse encounter details.
charity.decisiveQualification: Belief in bodily resurrection does not itself establish that the generating experiences were detailed physical encounters.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from ecstatic practices and sparse detail to a visionary explanation is coherent but needs a bridge from general community behavior to the specific appearances.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The span invokes scientific study and Pauline ecstatic activity, but provides no representative study details or close textual demonstration of the claimed regular hallucination pattern.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the affirmative's indispensable Pauline testimonial and bodily-encounter basis.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the distinction between bodily belief and encounter phenomenology, though it underdevelops affirmative textual evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes scientific studies of religious experiences and describes Pauline Christians as regularly entering ecstatic states, directly opposing the stronger physical-encounter reading.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The restricted pattern of appearances and Paul's exceptional conversion fit a localized visionary movement and cognitive dissonance better than a compassionate deity publicly revealing a saving resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier continues his uninterrupted opening, explicitly contrasting an ordinary natural movement with the proposed divine appearance.

components.text: Whether resurrection better explains the distribution of appearances to followers and a lone outsider.

response.rationale: The move presents restricted disclosure as unexpected under a compassionate deity and expected under a localized natural movement, directly opposing claimed explanatory superiority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts comparative expectations under the two hypotheses, although some psychological detail remains asserted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distribution argument is recoverable, but compassionate deity and public revelation require purpose-specific qualifications not supplied in the span.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Restricted appearances are relevant comparative evidence, but confidently inferring what a deity would do depends on unestablished assumptions about divine purposes.

charity.alternative: A deity could intentionally reveal the resurrection through selected witnesses rather than universal appearances.
charity.decisiveQualification: The affirmative must still explain why restricted disclosure is expected under the particular compassionate saving purpose attributed to the act.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The likelihood comparison is structurally coherent, but its divine-intention premise and the proposed natural movement's detailed fit are materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reported restricted pattern supplies some support, while cognitive dissonance and visionary-movement expectations are asserted without specific representative evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the motion tier, it directly argues that natural movement expectations outperform resurrection expectations for a central feature of the evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection identifies a real distributional challenge but weakens the purposive alternative by assuming near-universal disclosure.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts one small believer group and one outsider with worldwide continuing revelation, then identifies a natural movement as the more probable source of that restriction.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: A missing body becomes substantially more significant when joined to prior resurrection predictions, reputed miracles, and sincere appearance reports involving friends, foes, individuals, and groups.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona frames the example, develops the Koresh comparison, and ends by explicitly asking Carrier whether the added context changes the inference.

components.text: Whether a missing corpse remains weak evidence once it is combined with specific antecedent and testimonial evidence.

response.rationale: The analogy concedes that disappearance alone is insufficient and answers the threshold objection by proposing that predictions, miracle reputation, and varied sincere reports materially alter the evidential package.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive evidential demand but does not establish the reliability or independence of the added evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative principle is recoverable, but the selected excerpt is disfluent and does not itself state every element included in the locked proposition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The explicit concession about disappearance alone is well calibrated, though the degree to which the cumulative additions change the inference remains unsupported.

charity.alternative: Bodies can disappear for ordinary reasons, and extraordinary claims still require unusually reliable evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: The force of that objection depends on evaluating the cumulative package rather than treating the missing body in isolation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Cumulative evidence can rationally alter an inference, but the move compresses how the listed considerations interact and how strongly each is independently established.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Koresh and grandfather analogies illustrate the distinction, but the historical predictions, miracles, disappearance, and reports are not documented or independence-tested here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it attacks the evidential-threshold objection by specifying a cumulative evidential package rather than disappearance alone.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly concedes the ordinary disappearance point and narrows its answer to the proposed cumulative context.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly concedes that an ordinary missing body does not imply resurrection and begins an analogy intended to show why additional contextual claims would change the inference.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: A divine resurrection is an intentional act by a free agent and therefore belongs in a distinct reference class rather than the frequency class of naturally dead bodies.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly rejects Carrier's prior-probability treatment and articulates Licona's theistic free-agent reference-class argument.

components.text: Whether the frequency of naturally dead bodies supplies the appropriate prior reference class for an alleged divine act.

response.rationale: The move directly rejects the ordinary-death reference class by classifying resurrection as a purposive free-agent act, though it does not remove the need to assess the proposed agent and intention.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive reference-class premise while leaving the antecedent probability of divine agency unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument explicitly conditions its classification on resurrection being supernatural and probably performed by a deity for a specific purpose.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional classification is appropriately qualified, but calling the event a class by itself risks implying more prior-probability relief than uniqueness supplies.

charity.alternative: The rarity of resurrection remains evidentially relevant even if the event would be intentional.
charity.decisiveQualification: Intentional acts require reference to an agent's existence, capacities, motives, and opportunities rather than natural corpse frequencies alone.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reference-class distinction is coherent, but uniqueness alone does not yield a probability and the bridge to a favorable prior remains incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The intentional-action classification is conceptually supported by the hypothesis's content, while the existence and specific purpose of the proposed deity are not evidenced here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the con route's prior-probability treatment at a governing methodological point.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly identifies the natural-frequency objection and supplies a relevant intentional-action qualification without denying all prior assessment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt conditionally identifies resurrection as supernatural, probably performed by a deity for a specific purpose, and therefore involving a freely deciding agent.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Even a unique divine act depends on the prior probability that a god exists and intends that act, so uniqueness does not remove the resurrection's low prior.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier immediately answers Licona's reference-class claim and sustains the response through the extended exchange about inscrutability and prior probability.

components.text: Whether placing resurrection in a unique intentional-act class removes or neutralizes its antecedent improbability.

response.rationale: The reply directly states that the existence and particular intention of the proposed deity remain probability-bearing premises even if the act is unique.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the decisive inference from unique reference class to an inscrutable or neutral prior.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply clearly separates the prior for divine existence from the further prior for planning and executing this particular act.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is proportionate: it identifies probability-bearing conditions and rejects an automatic fifty-fifty assignment without pretending to calculate a precise prior.

charity.alternative: A unique free-agent act may resist frequency estimation from naturally dead bodies.
charity.decisiveQualification: Resistance to that frequency class does not eliminate priors concerning the agent's existence and specific intention.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is explicit and consistent: unique classification does not entail equal odds because the hypothesized agent and intention retain antecedent probabilities.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is conceptually strong, though no independent evidence or defended estimate is supplied for the divine-existence and intention priors.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supplies the con route's response to a major attempted defeat of the evidential-threshold bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response grants the relevant uniqueness point and identifies the precise probabilistic issue that remains.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly names God's existence, planning, and execution as prior-probability components and rejects treating a unique category as automatically yielding a fifty-fifty chance.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The appearance sequence can be explained as charismatic hallucinatory contagion in which Peter's private vision anchors and guides progressively larger groups into ecstatic visions.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier is directly asked what happened in the group appearances and develops a continuous, detailed causal reconstruction despite brief interlocutor challenges.

components.text: Whether one cause other than resurrection can explain the reported sequence of individual and group appearances.
Whether group appearance reports require corresponding shared physical encounters.

response.rationale: The move supplies a unified natural sequence beginning with a leader's private vision and extending through suggestion into group experiences, directly challenging resurrection's claimed explanatory advantage.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts both explanatory unity and group-experience demands, though the historical application remains schematic.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed sequence is clear, but contagious hallucination conflates suggestion, guided ecstatic experience, and potentially distinct individual perceptions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The mechanism is presented as an available explanation, but calling the sequence expected exceeds the unspecified studies and sparse historical linkage supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Leader suggestion could coordinate reports, but the move leaves material bridges from private vision to progressively larger group experiences and specific traditions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It invokes studies of hallucinatory contagion without representative details and does not establish that Peter or the reported groups underwent the proposed sequence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly advances the con route's natural-mechanisms bridge with a unified appearance-sequence proposal.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mainly constructs a natural mechanism and does not expressly analyze a sufficiently developed alternative within this span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly describes a leader's private vision, charismatic anchoring, inspiration, guidance, and suggestion as a contagious process producing the expected cult sequence.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Altered-state explanations poorly fit the reported ordinary-consciousness features and do not plausibly generate belief in a bodily resurrection associated with an empty grave.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona cites comparative research on consciousness states and then states his own central objection concerning bodily resurrection and the grave.

components.text: Whether altered-state and suggestion mechanisms fit the reported phenomenology closely enough to explain the appearances.
Whether the reports exhibit ordinary-consciousness characteristics inconsistent with a primarily ecstatic interpretation.

response.rationale: The reply applies ordinary-consciousness criteria to the reported appearances and argues that their characteristics mismatch the proposed altered-state mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the proposed psychological mechanism directly, though the reliability of the underlying narrative features remains untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ordinary-versus-altered-state comparison is clear and probabilistically framed, but which sources supply the six characteristics is not bounded in the excerpt.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The stated inverse relationship is qualified, yet six reported ordinary-consciousness qualities do not alone establish that an altered-state origin is unlikely.

charity.alternative: Altered-state experiences may contain ordinary-consciousness features or later acquire them in retelling.
charity.decisiveQualification: The natural account must still explain why multiple reported features cluster toward ordinary consciousness and bodily interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative mismatch inference is coherent, but it requires an uncompleted bridge from narrated characteristics to the original experiencers' actual states.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A stated ten-feature framework and six-feature application provide some specificity, while source reliability and validation of the diagnostic framework remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the con route's altered-state and contagious-vision mechanism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move addresses phenomenological fit but does not fully preserve the alternative possibility of mixed states or narrative development.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that increasing ordinary-consciousness characteristics reduce the likelihood of an altered state and reports that at least six of ten such qualities were identified in the appearances.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: Vision-driven believers could infer bodily resurrection without checking a grave, or reinterpret contrary bodily evidence through assumptions, denial, and conspiratorial rationalization.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier directly rejects Licona's assumptions about what the disciples knew or checked and develops several mechanisms for sustaining their belief.

components.text: Whether vision-driven believers could nevertheless form and preserve bodily-resurrection belief without grave confirmation.
Whether apparent bodily absence would reliably correct or prevent a mistaken resurrection inference.

response.rationale: The reply argues that committed religious groups can assume absence, deny contrary evidence, and rationalize it conspiratorially, thereby explaining bodily belief without verification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the grave-verification and bodily-inference issues, although it only indirectly answers the ordinary-consciousness evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed cognitive pathway is clear, but the extent to which modern cult behavior transfers to the earliest Christians remains implicitly qualified at best.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As a possibility claim, denial and conspiratorial rationalization are adequately supported by the stated behavioral analogy without claiming that this history certainly occurred.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed denial and rationalization process coherently permits bodily belief without verification, with a bounded historical-transfer gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move invokes observed cult behavior and a Matthew example, but offers no representative anthropological documentation or direct evidence that the earliest group followed this pathway.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly supplies the con bridge explaining bodily belief without reliable empty-grave verification.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span primarily establishes an available cognitive mechanism rather than evaluating a developed opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes believers assuming bodily absence, denying definitive contrary evidence, and using conspiratorial explanations, while invoking Matthew as an analogous rationalization example.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: The sacrifices and persecution endured by Paul and leading disciples provide evidence that they sincerely believed their Christian proclamation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker advances the pro-side argument from Paul's abandoned status, persecution, imprisonment, and reported martyrdom.

components.text: Whether early proclaimers' behavior supports sincere conviction rather than knowing fabrication or casual assumption.

response.rationale: The reply cites imprisonment, persecution, and the reported deaths of Peter, James, and Paul to establish sincere commitment, while not excluding sincere error.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts sincerity but leaves the opponent's decisive possibility of sincere mistaken belief substantially intact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is bounded to evidence of willingness and expressly distinguishes stronger evidence for three named figures from uncertainty about all disciples.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The express limits improve fit, though certainty about the named figures and martyrdom-based inference exceeds the documentation present in the span.

charity.alternative: Early proclaimers could be sincerely convinced yet factually mistaken about resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Costly perseverance supports sincerity but does not independently establish the truth or sensory basis of the belief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Costly persistence is relevant to sincere conviction, and the move avoids the invalid inference that willingness to die directly proves resurrection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The named imprisonments and deaths are asserted with useful qualification, but the span does not document the sources or establish what recantation opportunities existed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it materially supports the affirmative sincerity bridge while only weakly constraining sincere-error accounts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move is fair insofar as it argues sincerity rather than truth, though its placement only partially answers the mistaken-belief account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites imprisonment, persecution, and martyrdom, qualifies the evidence for the disciples generally, and identifies Peter, James, and Paul as the strongest named cases.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The earliest Christians probably believed they saw Jesus, although anthropological evidence means sincere proclamation cannot be treated as certain.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier explicitly states his probability judgment about lying, sincere belief, and what he infers from Paul's letters.

components.text: Whether costly proclamation establishes more than sincere belief and excludes deception or mistake.

response.rationale: The reply grants that sincere belief is more probable while explaining that sincerity is not certain and, more importantly, does not distinguish truth from mistake.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly concedes the supported sincerity inference and identifies the precise stronger conclusion that does not follow.

precisionFindings.rationale: The speaker clearly distinguishes probable sincere belief from absolute certainty and limits the anthropological point to evidential indistinguishability in some cases.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The probabilistic conclusion and express refusal of certainty closely match the limited anthropological and behavioral warrant supplied.

charity.alternative: Persecution and sacrifice provide genuine evidence that the leading proclaimers believed their message.
charity.decisiveQualification: Sincerity does not discriminate between a veridical resurrection encounter and a sincere visionary or mistaken interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The concession and limitation are explicit: probable sincerity is compatible with mistake, and similar evidence could sometimes arise even under deception.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The inference is supported by the behavioral evidence already discussed and an anthropological comparison, though that comparison is referenced rather than demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly advances the con explanation of sincere bodily belief without establishing the resurrection event.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the strongest warranted sincerity conclusion and confines its disagreement to certainty and truth implications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says sincere belief is more probable, rejects absolute certainty, and invokes anthropological cases where observed evidence could look similar even if participants were lying.

moves.speaker: Richard Carrier
moves.proposition: The Gospels are historically unreliable because external evidence, redactional embellishment, literary borrowing, and contradictions indicate mythmaking rather than history.
moves.attributionBasis: Carrier answers a direct request for one reason he distrusts the Gospels and develops multiple concrete historiographical examples.

components.text: Whether Gospel narrative characteristics can reliably recover the original appearance phenomenology used against altered-state explanations.
Whether Gospel empty-tomb detail provides historically reliable support for a missing body.

response.rationale: The move attacks reliance on Gospel phenomenology and empty-tomb material by citing external conflict, implausibility, literary construction, embellishment, and contradiction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the reliability of narrative evidence supporting both claims, although several indicators are only named rather than demonstrated.

precisionFindings.rationale: Specific indicators are identifiable, but the conclusion shifts from faults in selected episodes to historical unreliability of the Gospels as a whole without bounding the inference.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Some literary or historical problems can reduce reliability, but the categorical mythmaking conclusion outruns the briefly asserted examples and their uncertain scope.

charity.alternative: Ancient biographies may contain literary shaping and peripheral errors while preserving a historical narrative core.
charity.decisiveQualification: Core reliability still requires independent support and cannot simply be inferred after identifying embellishment and contradiction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The indicators are relevant to caution, but the move makes a substantial part-to-whole leap from selected problems to general Gospel unreliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It offers several potentially specific examples, including darkness and empty-tomb construction, but most are asserted without the external sources or comparative literary analysis needed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly attacks the historical usability of the Gospel core supporting embodied appearances and the empty grave.

representationalCharity.rationale: The critique identifies serious indicators but materially compresses the live possibility of mixed historical memory and literary development.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites externally disconfirmable darkness, claimed historical implausibility, literary construction, and an empty-tomb comparison as indicators of mythmaking and unreliable narration.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Ancient biographical freedom and contradictions in peripheral details do not by themselves discredit the Gospels' core account of the events they report.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona disputes Carrier's recommended authority, invokes ancient Gospel genre scholarship, and supplies the Titanic analogy.

components.text: Whether literary freedom, embellishment, and contradictions necessarily discredit the Gospels' central reported events.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes peripheral variation and ancient literary freedom from falsity of the narrative core, while conceding that some contradictions may remain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the inference from literary and peripheral defects to rejection of the core account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The core-versus-periphery distinction is clear and contradictions are conceded, but the content and boundary of the protected core are not specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that variation does not by itself discredit the core is appropriately cautious and expressly allows unresolved contradictions.
